title: Meet TVL (Total Value Locked)
objectives: What TVL measures, and what it is a proxy for
The three ways a TVL number gets inflated without new money arriving
How to judge liquidity depth yourself instead of trusting a headline

steps.title: What TVL measures
steps.body:
<Term id="tvl">TVL</Term> stands for total value locked: the dollar value of everything deposited into a protocol's contracts. Add up the vaults, convert to dollars, and you get one headline number.

People watch it on dashboards like DeFiLlama because it stands in for three things at once - how much capital users are willing to leave with a protocol, how much it's actually being used, and how deep the <Term id="liquidity_pool">liquidity</Term> is for trading or borrowing.

Keep it in proportion, though. TVL measures deposits, not quality. A protocol can be stuffed with TVL and still be a bad place to leave money. And, as the next section shows, that number is easier to inflate than it looks.

steps.title: Three ways TVL lies
steps.body:
The number is real. It's what goes into it that causes trouble.

**Double counting.** Deposit 10 SOL into a liquid staking protocol and you get a receipt token. Deposit that receipt into a lending market and the same capital now sits in two protocols' TVL at once. Stack a few layers and the same dollar can appear four times on a dashboard that's simply summing everything up.

**Self-priced assets.** A protocol locks a billion of its own governance token and values each one at the last traded price. If that price holds only because nobody is selling, "TVL" can be enormous and entirely illiquid. Sell $5,000 of it and you find out what it was really worth.

**Mercenary capital.** Yield hunters will park $50M in a farm for three days to collect emissions, then leave the instant the rewards slow. The TVL is high, the activity is real, and all of it is temporary.

None of that is necessarily fraud. It's that TVL measures a number the protocol controls, not a fact the chain forces on it.

steps.title: How the number is built
steps.body:
TVL isn't one on-chain value you can read off a contract. It's computed by an adapter - a small piece of code that knows where a given protocol keeps its funds.

For each vault, the adapter finds the token accounts, reads their balances, and multiplies by a price:

`TVL = sum of (token balance × price)`

The balances are hard data, and you can verify them yourself. The price is an assumption, and for a thinly traded token that assumption is doing most of the work.

Reputable dashboards let you toggle off double counting, staked governance tokens, and borrowed debt, so you can see how much of the headline survives. The habit worth building is small: when you see a TVL figure, ask what's inside it and who priced it.

questions.prompt: How can a protocol inflate its TVL without any real user money arriving?
options: By running its own RPC node
By minting unbacked tokens, pricing them on paper, and locking them in its own vaults
By deploying on Solana instead of Ethereum
By verifying its contract on an explorer
questions.explainRight: Self-minted tokens with no market, valued on paper and parked in the protocol's own contracts.
questions.explainWrong: Mint tokens nobody can sell, lock them in your own vaults, and let the paper price do the rest.

questions.prompt: What is 'double counting' in a TVL figure?
options: The same capital counted again each time it is deposited further down a stack of protocols
questions.explainRight: The same money counted once per protocol as it moves through wrapped and yield-bearing layers.
questions.explainWrong: It's one pile of capital appearing in several protocols' totals as it gets redeposited.
